requirements.text: The business must be able to identify each employee uniquely and consistently across all HR reporting.
Each employee carries a national identification number, described in the source system as unique, which is the strongest natural business identifier for a person.
Each employee is also registered under a company-wide business entity number that is shared with a broader business-entity register outside the HR area.
The warehouse must be able to reconcile the HR view of a person with the wider business-entity register.
Each employee has a network login identifying them in company IT systems; it may be used to join HR data to system-generated activity but must not be treated as the business identity of the person.
The technical row identifier used for data replication in the source system carries no business meaning and is not required for reporting.
The business must record the job title of each employee.
The business must record the hire date of each employee.
The business must be able to derive tenure (length of service) from the hire date.
The business must record whether each employee is salaried or hourly.
Salaried staff are exempt from collective bargaining and hourly staff are not.
Reporting must be able to distinguish salaried and hourly populations for both cost and labour-relations purposes.
The business must record whether each employee is currently active or inactive, as the operational statement of whether the person is presently employed.
Headcount reporting must be able to count only active employees, only inactive employees, or all people ever employed.
The business must record each employee's date of birth to support age-profile and workforce-planning analysis.
The business must record each employee's gender, recorded in the source as male or female.
The business must record each employee's marital status, recorded in the source as married or single.
Access to date of birth, gender and marital status in the warehouse must be restricted to authorised HR users, with exact restrictions subject to data-protection review.
Reporting for a wider audience must be possible without exposing personal attributes, for example by using age bands rather than birth dates.
The business must record each employee's available vacation hours.
The business must record each employee's available sick leave hours.
Leave balances are remaining entitlements at a point in time rather than accruals or consumption transactions, and reporting must be clear about the date to which any stated balance applies.
The business must be able to see how leave balances have moved over time in order to identify unusually high accrued balances and their associated liability.
The source area does not contain individual leave bookings, so leave balance movement can only be observed as a series of balance readings and not reconstructed from transactions.
The business must record where each employee sits in the corporate hierarchy, that is, who reports to whom, expressed as the employee's position within an organisational structure.
The business must record each employee's depth (level) in the hierarchy so that reporting can distinguish senior levels from front-line staff and aggregate to any chosen level.
The business must be able to report how many people report directly to a given manager.
The business must be able to report how many people report to a given manager in total at all levels below.
The business must be able to see the reporting structure as it stands today and, where the record permits, as it stood previously.
The source only carries the current hierarchy position for each employee, so reconstructing past structures depends on capturing changes as they occur.
The business must maintain a register of departments, the organisational units in which people work.
Each department is known by its name.
Each department belongs to a group, a larger organisational area, identified by the group's name.
Reporting must be able to aggregate any departmental measure (headcount, pay, movement) to the group level.
Departments can be created or retired, and department names and group memberships can be changed.
The business must know when a department's details were last changed.

The business wants to see figures both on today's departmental structure and on the departmental structure in force at the time, which requires capturing department history because the source holds only the current description.
The business must maintain a register of working shifts, each representing an eight-hour working period.
Each shift is known by its name (shift description).
The business must record the start time and end time of each shift.
Reporting must be able to analyse the workforce by shift, including how many people work each shift, in which departments, and how that has changed.

Shift definitions (name, start time, end time) can be adjusted, and the business needs to understand that a person recorded on a shift in the past may have worked different hours than a person recorded on the same-named shift today.
The business must record, for each employee, which department they worked in and on which shift, over time.
Each assignment must remain visible after it ends.
Each assignment records the date the employee started work in the department.
Each assignment records the date the employee left the department.
An assignment with no recorded leaving date is the employee's current department, and the business must be able to identify current assignments reliably on that basis.
The business must be able to state, for any given past date, which department and shift an employee was working in.
requirements.obj: employee department and shift at a date

requirements.text: The business must be able to produce headcount by department at any point in time, not merely today.
The business must be able to report movement between departments (transfers in, transfers out and net change) for any period, by department and by group.
The business must be able to report movement between shifts (transfers in, transfers out and net change) for any period.
The business must be able to measure how long an employee spends in a department before moving.
The business must be able to report the average length of assignment by department and by group.
An employee may hold the same department more than once at different times, and reporting must treat these as separate assignments rather than merging them.
An individual assignment is recognised in the source by the combination of employee, department, shift and start date.
Whether an employee may be assigned to more than one department at the same time is not settled by the schema and needs confirmation.
The business must record the pay rate of each employee and how it has changed over time, with each change remaining visible.
Each pay record carries the date on which the change in pay becomes effective, not the date the record was entered.
Each pay record carries the rate, expressed as an hourly rate in money terms.
Each pay record carries the pay frequency, either monthly or biweekly, which must be available for cost-phasing and payroll-cycle analysis.
The business must be able to state an employee's rate as at any given date by taking the rate whose effective date was most recent on or before that date.
The business must be able to report pay progression for an individual: the sequence of rates, the size of each change and the interval between changes.
The business must be able to report average, minimum and maximum rates by department, group, job title, shift and salaried/hourly classification at a chosen point in time.
requirements.obj: average, minimum and maximum pay rates

requirements.text: The business must be able to combine pay history with departmental assignment history so that a rate is attributed to the department the employee was working in when it applied.
The business must be able to analyse pay differences across groups of employees, such as between job titles or departments, in support of pay-equity review.
Any pay analysis touching gender or other personal attributes is subject to the access restrictions on personal data.

The conversion from hourly rate to periodic cost (contracted hours per period, treatment of salaried staff) is not stated in the source and must be confirmed with Payroll before any cost figure is published.
The business must record job candidates, people who applied for a position and whose application is held by HR.
Each candidate record carries the candidate's résumé, held as a structured document rather than as separate fields.
The business must at minimum know that a résumé exists and be able to retrieve it; extracting individual facts from within the résumé is not assumed.
A candidate record may be linked to an employee, and that link means the applicant was hired; where no employee is linked, the candidate was not hired or has not yet been hired.
The business must be able to report on hiring outcomes: how many candidates were recorded, how many were subsequently employed, and the conversion rate between the two.
The business must be able to trace an employed person back to the candidate record that preceded their employment, where one exists.
Not every employee has a candidate record; the source permits employees with no application on file.
Candidate records contain personal data of non-employees, and retention and access rules for them, likely different from those for employees, must be established before the data is published.
The source does not record the position applied for, an application date or a rejection reason, so recruitment-funnel reporting beyond the hired/not-hired outcome is not supported.
Every record in this area carries the date and time it was last updated in the operational system.
The business must be able to tell how current a given piece of information is and identify records that have not been touched for an unexpectedly long time.
Departmental and shift assignments and pay rates are changes for which the source system keeps a history, so the past is recoverable from the source itself.

An employee's job title, marital status, leave balances, active/inactive status, hierarchy position, and department and shift descriptions are overwritten in the source, so only the current value exists and any history must be built by observing changes as they occur.
The warehouse must preserve the succession of values for overwritten attributes so that questions such as how many people held a given job title at the end of last year become answerable in future.
Reporting must clearly distinguish as-is figures (using today's department structure and employee attributes) from as-was figures (using the structure and attributes in force at the time).
The business must be able to reproduce a previously published figure, so that re-running a report issued for a period gives the same answer despite later source corrections.
The business must be able to produce headcount and full-time-equivalent style summaries by department, group, shift, job title and salaried/hourly classification at a chosen date.
The business must be able to report joiners and leavers by period, derived from hire dates, the ending of assignments and the active/inactive status.
The business must be able to report tenure and age profiles of the workforce in bands.
The business must be able to report internal mobility: how many people changed department or shift in a period and the flows between specific departments.
The business must be able to report pay-rate distribution and progression by department, group, job title, shift and salaried/hourly classification.
The business must be able to report accrued vacation and sick-leave balances by department and group as an indicator of liability.
The business must be able to report recruitment conversion as the proportion of recorded candidates who were subsequently employed.

business_keys.rationale: REQ-002 describes the national identification number as unique and the strongest natural business identifier for a person; REQ-001 requires unique, consistent identification. It is business-recognised and stable, though nullability is not explicitly confirmed.

REQ-003 and REQ-004 state each employee is registered under a company-wide business entity number shared with the wider register, which is needed for reconciliation. It is a business-recognised, stable identifier, but is less strongly called unique/identifying than the national ID, so it ranks second.

REQ-005 says the network login identifies the person in IT systems and may be used for joins, but must not be treated as the person's business identity. It is a weak candidate and may change over time.
REQ-032 says each department is known by its name, so it is the business-recognised identifier. REQ-035 says names can change, which hurts stability.

The source column DepartmentID is used to reference departments in assignments (REQ-043, REQ-055). It is stable, but the requirements do not call it a business-recognised identifier, so it is more like a system-assigned key.
REQ-039 says each shift is known by its name (shift description). REQ-042 says shift definitions can be adjusted, which weakens stability.
The source column ShiftID is referenced in assignments (REQ-055). It is stable, but the requirements do not call it a business-recognised key, so it is more like a system-assigned key.

REQ-068 requires recording candidates, but the requirements name no natural identifier for them. JobCandidateID is the only listed source identifier and is probably system-generated, so the score is low.

REQ-055 says an individual assignment is recognised in the source by the combination of employee, department, shift and start date. REQ-054 requires repeat stints in the same department to be kept as separate assignments.
REQ-057, REQ-058 and REQ-061 identify a pay record by employee and the effective date of the rate change. The requirements do not state explicitly that this combination is unique.

satellites.description: The employee's position and level in the organisational hierarchy. History is captured as changes occur.
satellites.split_rationale: Hierarchy position is its own concern and changes on a different schedule from other attributes.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_pay_history
satellites.description: Pay rate history. RateChangeDate (the effective date) separates the concurrent records.
satellites.split_rationale: Comes from a separate source table at a finer grain (one row per rate change). EmployeePayHistory is now declared as a feed of hub_business_entity.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_department_shift_effectivity
satellites.description: Active period of each department/shift assignment. An assignment with no end date is the current one.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_department_shift_audit
satellites.description: When each assignment record was last updated, used to judge how current it is.
satellites.split_rationale: The audit timestamp is kept apart from the effectivity dates.

satellites.name: sat_department_details
satellites.description: Department name, group membership and last-change date. History is kept for as-was reporting.

satellites.name: sat_shift_details
satellites.description: Shift name and start/end times. History is kept because definitions can be adjusted.

satellites.name: sat_job_candidate_resume
satellites.description: The candidate's résumé, stored as a structured document. It is non-employee personal data, subject to its own retention rules.

contracts.name: Department
contracts.doc: Source-to-staging asset representing organizational departments (HumanResources Department). Each record identifies a department, its name, the group it belongs to, and when the record was last modified. The contract enforces the declared schema, business key (DepartmentID) and not-null rules; value-level semantics are only asserted where a requirement supports them. Ownership and agreement are pending human review.

schema.name: DepartmentID
schema.description: Identifier of the department; the business key of the Department asset.

schema.name: Name
schema.description: Name of the department.

schema.name: GroupName
schema.description: Name of the department group to which the department belongs.

schema.name: ModifiedDate
schema.description: Date and time the department record was last modified in the source.

contracts.name: Employee
contracts.doc: Employee master record from the source system, one row per employee, identified by BusinessEntityID. Draft contract: schema, primary-key and not-null breaches are enforced as hard by the core; value-level semantics are advisory (soft) pending producer/consumer review.

schema.name: BusinessEntityID
schema.description: Unique identifier of the employee (business entity) in the source system.

schema.name: NationalIDNumber
schema.description: National identification number (e.g. government-issued ID) of the employee.

schema.name: LoginID
schema.description: Network login identifier of the employee.

schema.name: OrganizationNode
schema.description: Position of the employee in the organizational hierarchy.

schema.name: OrganizationLevel
schema.description: Depth of the employee in the organizational hierarchy.

schema.name: JobTitle
schema.description: Work title of the employee.

schema.name: BirthDate
schema.description: Employee date of birth.

schema.name: MaritalStatus
schema.description: Marital status code of the employee.

schema.name: Gender
schema.description: Gender code of the employee.

schema.name: HireDate
schema.description: Date the employee was hired.

schema.name: SalariedFlag
schema.description: Indicates whether the employee is salaried (as opposed to hourly).

schema.name: VacationHours
schema.description: Number of vacation hours available to the employee.

schema.name: SickLeaveHours
schema.description: Number of sick leave hours available to the employee.

schema.name: CurrentFlag
schema.description: Indicates whether the employee record is currently active.

schema.name: rowguid
schema.description: Globally unique row identifier (GUID) for the record.

schema.name: ModifiedDate
schema.description: Date and time the record was last modified.

contracts.name: EmployeeDepartmentHistory
contracts.doc: Source-to-staging asset recording the history of departments and shifts to which each employee has been assigned over time, with start and end dates for each assignment. The contract enforces the declared schema and business-key integrity; value-level constraints are left for producer/consumer negotiation at the human review checkpoint.

schema.name: BusinessEntityID
schema.description: Identifier of the employee (business entity) the department assignment belongs to; references Employee.BusinessEntityID.

schema.name: DepartmentID
schema.description: Identifier of the department the employee was assigned to; references Department.DepartmentID.

schema.name: ShiftID
schema.description: Identifier of the work shift the employee was assigned to; references Shift.ShiftID.

schema.name: StartDate
schema.description: Date the employee started working in the department and shift.

schema.name: EndDate
schema.description: Date the employee stopped working in the department and shift; empty when the assignment is current.

schema.name: ModifiedDate
schema.description: Date and time the record was last modified in the source system.

contracts.name: EmployeePayHistory
contracts.doc: Employee pay history: one record per employee pay-rate change, identifying the employee, the date the rate changed, the new rate, and the pay frequency. The contract enforces the declared schema, business-key uniqueness and not-null constraints; no value-level thresholds are stated in the requirements.

schema.name: BusinessEntityID
schema.description: Identifier of the employee whose pay rate changed; refers to the employee's business entity.

schema.name: RateChangeDate
schema.description: Date on which the employee's pay rate change took effect.

schema.name: Rate
schema.description: Pay rate for the employee as of the rate change date. Currency and unit are not specified in the requirements.

schema.name: PayFrequency
schema.description: Code indicating how often the employee is paid. The allowed values are not specified in the requirements.

schema.name: ModifiedDate
schema.description: Date and time the record was last modified in the source.

contracts.name: JobCandidate
contracts.doc: Source-to-staging asset for job candidates (HumanResources.JobCandidate). Each record represents a candidate's submitted resume, optionally linked to an employee via BusinessEntityID. The contract enforces the declared schema, business keys and not-null rules; value-level semantics are alerting-only unless a requirement mandates otherwise. Ownership and agreement are to be confirmed at the human-in-the-loop checkpoint.

schema.name: JobCandidateID
schema.description: Identifier of the job candidate record.

schema.name: BusinessEntityID
schema.description: Identifier of the employee the candidate was hired as, referencing the Employee business entity. May be absent for candidates who were not hired.

schema.name: Resume
schema.description: Candidate's resume content as submitted. Format of the content is not specified in the requirements.

schema.name: ModifiedDate
schema.description: Date and time the record was last modified in the source.

contracts.name: Shift
contracts.doc: Work shift reference data from the source Shift table, describing each shift's name and daily start and end times. The contract enforces the declared schema, the business key (ShiftID) and not-null rules. Ownership and agreement are pending human review.

schema.name: ShiftID
schema.description: Identifier of the shift; business key of the Shift asset.

schema.name: Name
schema.description: Name of the shift.

schema.name: StartTime
schema.description: Time of day at which the shift starts.

schema.name: EndTime
schema.description: Time of day at which the shift ends.

schema.name: ModifiedDate
schema.description: Date and time the source record was last modified.
